newsitem.title: USA: Indictment of prosecutors, cops shocks legal world.
newsitem.headline: Indictment of prosecutors, cops shocks legal world.

text.p: Charges that three former prosecutors and four sheriff's police framed a man who spent nearly a decade on death row sent shockwaves through the law enforcement world Friday.

"Criminal charges like these are exceptionally unusual. I can't think of another case where prosecutors were charged with hiding or making up evidence," said Patrick Cotter, a former federal prosecutor who is a professor at Chicago-Kent College of Law.

The case could dampen if not chill the zeal of prosecutors across the country if those involved in the case are held liable for what amounts to judgment calls, rather than for something more deliberate and blatant, Cotter added.

Indictments announced Thursday alleged that three former county prosecutors in suburban Chicago's DuPage County presented testimony they knew to be false or withheld from defence lawyers information that might have exonerated the murder suspect, Rolando Cruz.
The sheriff's officers were accused variously of perjury and obstruction of justice.

Cruz was twice found guilty and sentenced to death in the killing of 10-year-old Jeanine Nicarico in her home in 1983. The two convictions were reversed and when Cruz was being tried a third time the trial judge acquitted him, saying false testimony had been presented.
The indictments resulted from the appointment of a special prosecutor to investigate how the case was handled.

"If it's just a mistake, that's real chilling," added Cotter, commenting on the case. "As a prosecutor you're at the mercy of your witnesses ... you can't call central casting for a witness, you've got to take them where you find them.

"But if they're being prosecuted for knowingly hiding evidence or putting false evidence on the stand, that's not terribly chilling because most prosecutors would never be stupid as to do something like that ... it's not worth it," he added.

The murder case remains officially unsolved, though reports over the years have said a man jailed for another crime confessed to it under hypnosis. The victim's father, Thomas Nicarico, defended the prosecution of the case, saying he and his wife "can't imagine they did or would railroad an innocent man."

Paul Petterson, acting general counsel for the National Association of Criminal Defence Lawyers, told the Chicago Tribune the indictments present a "fox-guarding-the-henhouse problem ... Who's going to prosecute the prosecutor?"

A lawyer representing Thomas Knight, one of the former prosecutors named in the indictments, said, "Every police officer and prosecutor in this country should be outraged ... murderers are being made into martyrs."
